title: Data Structures in C
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs expect candidates to build and reason about arrays, lists, trees, and hash tables from structs, pointers, and malloc in C.

phases.goal: Establish that C has no built-in containers and that core structures are defined with structs, pointers, and heap allocation.

must_hit.point: C has no standard containers like vector or List; you build them from structs, pointers, and malloc.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states you implement containers yourself with structs/pointers/malloc rather than using a language-provided vector or list type.

must_hit.point: A dynamic array is tracked with a heap data pointer plus current length and total capacity (e.g. int_vec_t with data, len, cap).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names the three fields: pointer to allocated memory, len, and cap.

must_hit.point: A singly linked list node is self-referential: data plus a next pointer, with the last node pointing to NULL.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes struct node { val; next; } and NULL as the end sentinel.

must_hit.point: A BST node holds left and right child pointers and obeys: all left-subtree values < N and all right-subtree values > N.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the left/right fields and the strict ordering rule around node N.

must_hit.point: A hash table maps a key to a bucket index via a hash function over a dynamically allocated array of buckets.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions hash function → integer index into an array of buckets.

probes: Why can't you just use a fixed-size array when the number of items is unknown, and what fields would you put in a dynamic-array struct?
What does a singly linked list node store, and how do you know you've reached the end?

hints.1: Think about what C gives you out of the box versus what you allocate on the heap.
hints.2: Contrast a rigid int arr[N] with a struct that tracks a pointer, how many slots are used, and how many are allocated.
hints.3: Dynamic array: data/len/cap. Linked list: val + next, last next is NULL. No std::vector in C—build it with malloc.

phases.goal: Explain how dynamic arrays grow, how list/BST/hash/ring-buffer operations update pointers and memory, and how common list algorithms preserve the chain.

must_hit.point: When len == cap, grow by allocating a larger block (often cap * 2), copy elements over (memcpy or realloc), and free the old block; amortized doubling keeps append O(1) on average despite occasional O(n) copies.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the full-capacity resize path with doubling and amortized O(1) append.

must_hit.point: Before free(current) when deleting or freeing a list, stash current->next in a temporary; after free, current->next is unreadable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate saves next first, then frees, then advances—never free then read through the freed pointer.

must_hit.point: A circular/ring buffer uses a fixed-size array and head/tail indices that wrap to zero with modulo (%), giving O(1) enqueue/dequeue without shifting or malloc.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions fixed array, head and tail, wrap with %, no element shifting.

must_hit.point: BST deletion has three cases: leaf → free and NULL parent link; one child → relink parent to that child then free; two children → replace with in-order successor (smallest in right subtree) then delete the successor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate enumerates leaf / one-child / two-child and names in-order successor for the two-child case.

must_hit.point: Hash collisions are commonly resolved in C with separate chaining (each bucket is a linked list); when load factor (entries/buckets) exceeds a threshold (often 0.75), allocate a larger array and re-hash all keys.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes chaining lists per bucket and rehash when load factor crosses the stated threshold.

must_hit.point: Iterative list reverse uses three pointers (prev, curr, next): save next, reverse curr->next to prev, then advance prev and curr.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks the three-pointer reverse loop and returns prev as the new head.

probes: Walk through what happens on append when a dynamic array is full.
How do you free an entire linked list without leaking or use-after-free?
How does a ring buffer enqueue without shifting elements?

hints.1: Focus on what must be saved or recomputed before any free or wrap-around.
hints.2: Resize: new capacity, copy, free old. List free/delete: temporary next. Ring: head/tail and %.
hints.3: len==cap → often cap*2 via realloc/memcpy; stash next before free(curr); ring uses % wrap; hash uses chaining and rehash past load factor often 0.75.

phases.goal: Compare structure choices for access patterns, insert/delete cost, and who owns pointed-to memory.

must_hit.point: Singly linked lists shine for frequent mid-sequence insert/delete (pointer updates only, no shifting) but break for rapid random access because you must traverse from the head.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts O(1)* local pointer updates vs inability to jump to the i-th element without walking.

must_hit.point: A doubly linked list adds prev for bidirectional traversal and O(1) deletion if you already hold the node, at the cost of managing more pointers per operation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names prev, both-direction walk, cheaper delete when node is known, more pointer bookkeeping.

must_hit.point: Stacks/queues are abstract: array-backed stack only pushes/pops at the end; list-backed queue keeps head (dequeue) and tail (enqueue); embedded systems often prefer a ring buffer when malloc is unavailable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps LIFO/FIFO backends and cites circular buffer as the no-malloc queue.

must_hit.point: Memory ownership must be explicit: if the list owns data, list_free frees node->data then the node; if it only borrows, the caller frees data and the list frees only node structs—or you get double-frees/leaks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes owning vs borrowing and ties it to who calls free on payload vs node.

probes: When would you pick a linked list over a dynamic array, and when would that choice fail?
Who should call free on the data inside a list node?

hints.1: Ask what operation dominates: middle edits vs indexing by position.
hints.2: List: pointer rewiring, no shift, no random access. Ownership: own payload vs borrow references.
hints.3: Mid insert/delete → list; random access → array. Doubly linked: O(1) delete with node pointer. Document own vs borrow to avoid double-free/leak.

phases.goal: Apply classic interview patterns on lists and trees using the structures' pointer mechanics.

must_hit.point: Detect a linked-list cycle with Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one step, fast moves two; same node means a cycle, fast hitting NULL means none.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names two-pointer speeds and both termination conditions.

must_hit.point: Find the middle of a list with the same slow/fast pointer trick.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says advance fast twice as fast as slow; slow lands near the middle.

must_hit.point: Validate a binary tree as a BST by tracking allowed min and max during recursive descent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes tightening min/max bounds as you recurse left and right.

must_hit.point: In-order traversal of a BST (left, current, right) yields a sorted sequence because of the BST ordering property.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate links left-then-node-then-right to sorted output via the left < N < right rule.

must_hit.point: A standard BST can degenerate into a linked list on already-sorted inserts (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4), turning search from O(log n) into O(n); balanced trees (Red-Black, AVL) keep O(log n) depth.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains skewed insertion → chain shape and names rebalancing variants as the fix.

probes: How do you detect a cycle in a singly linked list?
Why can inserting sorted keys into a plain BST destroy logarithmic search?
How would you check whether a binary tree is a valid BST?

hints.1: Think about two cursors moving at different speeds, or about bounds on recursive tree walks.
hints.2: Cycle/middle: slow one step, fast two. BST validity: pass down min/max. Degeneration: always go right on sorted input.
hints.3: Floyd: meet ⇒ cycle, fast NULL ⇒ none. Sorted inserts 1,2,3,4 ⇒ right spine, O(n) search; use AVL/Red-Black. In-order is sorted because of BST order.

tradeoffs.topic: Dynamic array vs singly linked list
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays give contiguous storage and O(1) access to the i-th element but insert/delete need shifting (O(n)); linked lists update a few pointers for mid-sequence insert/delete (O(1) with a pointer to the preceding node) but access and search are O(n) because you walk from the head.
Doubly linked lists add a prev pointer for bidirectional traversal and O(1) deletion when you already have the node, paid for by extra pointer updates on every structural change.

tradeoffs.topic: Array-backed stack / list-backed queue vs ring buffer
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Stacks and queues can sit on dynamic arrays or linked lists (stack: push/pop at end; queue: head for dequeue, tail for enqueue). Without malloc, a fixed-size circular buffer with head/tail and modulo wrap gives O(1) enqueue/dequeue with no shifting.

tradeoffs.topic: BST vs hash table for lookup
tradeoffs.strong_answer: BSTs give O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced and support sorted iteration via in-order traversal; hash tables target O(1) average lookup via hashing into buckets, with separate chaining and rehashing when load factor grows too high.

tradeoffs.topic: Owning vs borrowing memory in node-based containers
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If the container owns payloads, free must release node->data then the node; if it borrows, only node structs are freed and the caller frees data—otherwise you risk double-frees or leaks. Generics with void* also need caller-supplied compare/free function pointers because the container cannot interpret opaque pointers.

gotchas.trap: Updating or freeing a list pointer before saving its successor (e.g. free(current); current = current->next).
gotchas.correction: Stash next in a temporary before free, then advance; otherwise the rest of the list is lost (leak) and reading through the freed node is invalid.

gotchas.trap: Traversing a list by moving the head pointer itself.
gotchas.correction: Walk with a separate current pointer so the original head remains available.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a plain BST always searches in O(log n).
gotchas.correction: Sorted insertion (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4) makes every node a right child, degenerating into a linked list with O(n) search; use self-balancing trees (Red-Black, AVL) for guaranteed O(log n) depth.

gotchas.trap: Leaving ownership of void* / node payloads undefined.
gotchas.correction: Document whether the container owns or borrows data, and pass function pointers (compare, free_element) for generic containers so free and ordering are well-defined.
